Pilot Sample Size for Two Stage Bounded Risk Estimation of a Normal Mean

Source: R/ts_br_norm_mean.R
ts_br_norm_mean_pilot.Rd

Returns the first stage (pilot) sample size for the two stage bounded risk point estimation procedure for the mean of a normal distribution, evaluated by ts_br_norm_mean. The loss in estimating the mean \(\mu\) by the sample mean is \(A\,|\bar{X} - \mu|^k\), and the procedure keeps its expectation, the risk, at or below w.

Usage

ts_br_norm_mean_pilot(A, k, w, m_0 = 10, gamma = 1)

Arguments

A

The loss constant: the loss is \(A\,|\bar{X} - \mu|^k\). A single positive number, in the units of w per unit of error to the power k.

k

The error index: 1 for absolute error loss, 2 for squared error loss.

w

The risk bound: the largest acceptable expected loss. A single positive number.

m_0

The smallest first stage sample size to return. A whole number of at least \(k + 2\). Default 10; see Details.

gamma

Positive tuning constant of the pilot rule. Larger values give a smaller first stage. Default 1.

Value

A length one integer: the first stage sample size.

Details

The pilot size is $$m = \max\{m_0,\ \lceil ((B / w)^{2/k})^{1/(1 + \gamma)} \rceil\}, \qquad B = A \, \frac{2^{k/2}}{\sqrt{\pi}} \, \Gamma\!\left(\frac{k + 1}{2}\right),$$ where \(B = A\,E|Z|^k\) for a standard normal \(Z\), which is \(A\) for \(k = 2\) and \(A\sqrt{2/\pi}\) for \(k = 1\). (For \(k = 2\) and the default \(\gamma = 1\) the rule is therefore \(\lceil \sqrt{A / w} \rceil\).) The sample size that would be used if the variance \(\sigma^2\) were known is \(n^* = (B / w)^{2/k} \sigma^2\); the rule raises the constant \((B / w)^{2/k}\) to the power \(1/(1 + \gamma)\), so the first stage grows with the size of the problem but more slowly than \(n^*\) does. This is the form of pilot that Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, Equation 24) recommend, following Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009), for a purely sequential procedure. Using it here, with \(n^*\) for \(\sigma = 1\) as the constant, is this package's choice and not part of the two stage procedure. A pilot equal to \((B / w)^{2/k}\) itself, the optimal sample size for \(\sigma = 1\), would exceed \(n^*\) whenever \(\sigma\) is below 1. The rule's first stage exceeds \(n^*\) only when \(\sigma^2\) is below \(((B / w)^{2/k})^{-\gamma/(1 + \gamma)}\), a threshold that shrinks as the problem grows.

The minimum m_0 matters more than the rule. The procedure is defined only for a first stage of at least \(k + 2\) observations, and it pays for not knowing the variance through a constant that is large when the first stage is small: the expected total sample size is about \(b_m^{2/k}\) times \(n^*\) (see ts_br_norm_mean for \(b_m\)). For squared error (\(k = 2\)) that ratio is \((m - 1)/(m - 3)\): 3 for \(m = 4\), 2 for \(m = 5\), 1.29 for \(m = 10\), and 1.12 for \(m = 20\). For absolute error (\(k = 1\)) it is 3.14 for \(m = 3\), 1.57 for \(m = 5\), 1.20 for \(m = 10\), and 1.09 for \(m = 20\). The default m_0 = 10 holds the expected total to about 1.3 times \(n^*\). A first stage larger than \(n^*\) is wasted, so lower m_0 only when even ten observations may be more than the study needs.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean waiting time, squared error loss, mean squared error at most 4.
ts_br_norm_mean_pilot(A = 1, k = 2, w = 4)
#> [1] 10

# A demanding bound: the rule exceeds the minimum.
ts_br_norm_mean_pilot(A = 1, k = 2, w = 0.001)
#> [1] 32
